Consequently, EdgePoint2 emerges as a highly competitive option for visual tasks, especially in contexts demanding adaptability to diverse computational and communication constraints.Demo and weights are available at https://github.com/HITCSC/EdgePoint2.

title: DogMo: A Large-Scale Multi-View RGB-D Dataset for 4D Canine Motion Recovery
abstract: We present DogMo , a large-scale multi-view RGB-D video dataset capturing diverse canine movements for real canine motion recovery. DogMo comprises \(1.2k\) motion sequences collected from \(10\) unique dog instances, covering \(11\) action types and over \(220\) minutes of recordings. Each motion is captured by five synchronized RGB-D cameras, providing multi-view RGB-D observations, masks, keypoints, and action labels. Compared with existing dog datasets, DogMo offers rich variation in both motion and breed, provides synchronized multi-view RGB-D observations at a larger scale, and supports systematic evaluation for real canine motion recovery. Leveraging DogMo , we establish four motion recovery benchmark settings that support evaluation across monocular and multi-view, RGB and RGB-D inputs. We also provide a three-stage, instance-specific fitting pipeline, which produces observation-consistent SMAL-based canine motion annotations by progressively refining dog body shape and pose through coarse alignment, dense correspondence supervision, and temporal regularization. We hope DogMo can facilitate future research on animal motion recovery, multi-view reconstruction, and animal behavior modeling.

title: Flexible Focus Sampling for Depth from Focus
abstract: Depth from Focus (DfF) acquires depth cues of 3D scenes through focus sampling at different focal planes, with its core principle being the mapping between focus and depth. Existing DfF methods generally assume dense and fixed focus sampling to ensure complete coverage and consistent focus-depth mapping. However, this assumption restricts practical deployment because the depth range of scenes varies significantly, and enforcing uniform dense sampling across all cases leads to severe inefficiency. Motivated by this challenge, we theoretically analyze focus response curves under different sampling intervals and reveal the phenomenon of sampling neighborhood alleviation. This phenomenon indicates that focus response curves remain similar within neighboring sampling intervals, thereby maintaining a stable focus-depth mapping. Based on this property, we further derive a generalization principle for multiple sampling intervals, which guides the selection of representative intervals to efficiently cover diverse sampling patterns through their neighborhoods. This analysis provides a theoretical basis for interpreting focus sampling from a generalization perspective, thereby enabling practical flexible focus sampling. Accordingly, we propose the Flexible Focus Sampling DfF (FFS-DfF) framework, which trains the proposed Mamba U-Net (MU-Net) using representative-interval samples and further employs Pareto optimization to balance performance across intervals. Extensive experiments show that FFS-DfF achieves superior sampling-agnostic robustness over existing DfF methods. The code is available at https://github.com/jiangfeng-Z/FFS-DfF .

title: BBoxMaskPose v2: Expanding Mutual Conditioning to 3D
abstract: Most 2D human pose estimation benchmarks are nearly saturated, with the exception of crowded scenes. We introduce PMPose, a top-down 2D pose estimator that incorporates the probabilistic formulation and the mask-conditioning. PMPose improves crowded pose estimation without sacrificing performance on standard scenes. Building on this, we present BBoxMaskPose v2 (BMPv2) integrating PMPose and an enhanced SAM-based mask refinement module. BMPv2 surpasses state-of-the-art by 1.5 average precision (AP) points on COCO and 6 AP points on OCHuman, becoming the first method to exceed 50 AP on OCHuman. We demonstrate that BMP’s 2D prompting of 3D model improves 3D pose estimation in crowded scenes and that advances in 2D pose quality directly benefit 3D estimation. Results on the new OCHuman-Pose dataset show that multi-person performance is more affected by pose prediction accuracy than by detection. The code, models, and data are available on the project website .

title: Saving for the Future: Enhancing Generalization via Partial Logic Regularization
abstract: Generalization remains a significant challenge in visual classification tasks, particularly in handling unknown classes in real-world applications. Existing research focuses on the class discovery paradigm, which tends to favor known classes, and the incremental learning paradigm, which suffers from catastrophic forgetting. Recent approaches, such as the L-Reg technique, employ logic-based regularization to enhance generalization but are bound by the necessity of fully defined logical formulas, limiting flexibility for unknown classes. This paper introduces PL-Reg, a novel partial-logic regularization term that allows models to reserve space for undefined logic formulas, improving adaptability to unknown classes. Specifically, it is demonstrated that tasks involving unknown classes can be effectively explained using partial logic. An idealized analysis is also presented, motivating why partial logic may help preserve generalization capacity for unknown classes. We evaluate PL-Reg through extensive experiments on Generalized Category Discovery, Multi-Domain Generalized Category Discovery, long-tailed Class Incremental Learning, and Continual Category Discovery, and observe improvements across the evaluated settings, with gains of varying magnitudes. Our results highlight the effectiveness of partial logic in tackling challenges related to unknown classes.

title: Accurate and Efficient Object Pose Estimation via the Aggregation of Diffusion Features
abstract: Estimating the pose of objects from images is a crucial task of 3D scene understanding, and recent approaches have shown promising results on very large benchmarks. However, these methods experience a significant performance drop when dealing with unseen objects. We believe that it results from the limited generalizability of image features. To address this problem, we have an in-depth analysis on the features of diffusion models, e.g. Stable Diffusion, which hold substantial potential for modeling unseen objects. Based on this analysis, we then innovatively introduce these diffusion features for object pose estimation. To achieve this, we propose three distinct architectures that can effectively capture and aggregate diffusion features of different granularity, greatly improving the generalizability of object pose estimation. Our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by a considerable margin on three popular benchmark datasets, LM, O-LM, and T-LESS. In particular, our method achieves higher accuracy than the previous best arts on unseen objects: 98.2% vs. 93.5% on Unseen LM, 85.9% vs. 76.3% on Unseen O-LM, showing the strong generalizability of our method. Our code is released at https://github.com/Tianfu18/diff-feats-pose.

title: Image-to-Video Transfer Learning based on Image-Language Foundation Models: A Comprehensive Survey
abstract: Image-Language Foundation Models (ILFMs) provide transferable multimodal representations that generalize well across diverse downstream image-based tasks. The advancement of video-text research has spurred growing interest in extending image-based models to the video domain. This paradigm, termed image-to-video transfer learning, effectively reduces the data and computational costs of training video-language models while achieving comparable or even superior performance to training from scratch. This survey provides the first comprehensive review of this emerging field. We begin by summarizing the widely used ILFMs and their capabilities. We then systematically classify existing image-to-video transfer learning techniques into two broad categories, namely frozen parameters and adapted parameters, according to whether the ILFM parameters are kept frozen or directly updated during transfer. In the frozen-parameter paradigm, the original ILFM parameters remain fixed, while task-specific modules, side networks, adapters, LoRA modules, prompts, or post-networks can be trained to bridge the image-to-video gap. In the adapted-parameter paradigm, part or all of the ILFM backbone is updated to produce video-adapted representations for downstream video tasks. Given the task- and benchmark-dependent requirements of image-to-video transfer, this survey systematically reviews these strategies and discusses their applications across a wide range of video-text tasks, from fine-grained tasks with localized spatio-temporal outputs, such as spatio-temporal video grounding, to coarse-grained tasks with global or textual outputs, such as video question answering. We further present a detailed experimental analysis to investigate the efficacy of different image-to-video transfer learning paradigms on a range of downstream video understanding tasks. Finally, we summarize the key challenges and discuss promising future directions. By providing a comprehensive and structured overview, this survey aims to serve as a roadmap for advancing video-text learning through the adaptation of image-language foundation models, while also supporting future research in this rapidly evolving field. Additional resources and the latest updates are available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/YuriPreisdent/awesome-image-to-video-transfer .
